subject: Environment
description: Air, water, soil pollution indicators; greenhouse gases; major treaties

questions.stem: The GREENHOUSE GAS with the HIGHEST contribution to global warming by volume in the atmosphere is:
questions.explanation: CO₂ contributes ~76% of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions (largest absolute contribution). Methane is ~16% but ~28× more potent per molecule over 100 years (GWP). N₂O is 6%, HFCs/PFCs/SF₆ make up the rest but with very high GWPs.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The primary pollutant responsible for ACID RAIN is:

options.option_text: Sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen

questions.explanation: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ / H₂SO₄; NOₓ → HNO₃. These lower rain pH below 5.6. Major sources: coal-fired power plants, vehicles. CFCs destroy stratospheric ozone; ground-level ozone is a pollutant but not the cause of acid rain.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Match the INTERNATIONAL ENVIRONMENTAL TREATY with its PURPOSE. A. Montreal Protocol (1987). B. Kyoto Protocol (1997). C. Paris Agreement (2015). D. Ramsar Convention (1971). List-II: 1. Phase-out of ozone-depleting substances (CFCs). 2. Conservation of wetlands of international importance. 3. Legally binding emission-reduction targets for developed nations. 4. Global pact to limit warming to well below 2 °C, ideally 1.5 °C.
questions.explanation: Montreal — ozone layer (CFCs). Kyoto — binding on Annex-I countries only, 2008-2012 commitment period. Paris — nationally-determined contributions (NDCs), global stocktake every 5 years. Ramsar — wetlands, named after Ramsar (Iran) where it was signed.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) is a measure of:

options.option_text: Oxygen required by fish to breathe
Oxygen consumed by microorganisms to decompose organic matter in water
Oxygen released by aquatic plants in photosynthesis
Oxygen dissolved in atmospheric air above water

questions.explanation: BOD is the dissolved oxygen consumed by aerobic microorganisms breaking down organic matter, over a specified period (usually 5 days at 20 °C → BOD₅). HIGH BOD = HIGH organic pollution = LOW dissolved oxygen left for aquatic life. Sewage-polluted water typically shows BOD > 30 mg/L.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Consider the following about PM 2.5. 1. It refers to particulate matter 2.5 micrometres or smaller in aerodynamic diameter. 2. It can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. 3. Major sources include vehicle exhaust, construction dust, and biomass burning. 4. The WHO's revised (2021) annual guideline value is 5 µg/m³. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: All four correct. PM 2.5 is a major culprit in the winter-smog crisis of Delhi-NCR. India's NAAQS annual limit is 40 µg/m³ — much higher than WHO's 5 µg/m³, and typical Delhi winters exceed 100 µg/m³.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: EUTROPHICATION of a lake refers to:

options.option_text: Nutrient enrichment causing algal blooms and oxygen depletion
Rise in water temperature due to industrial discharge

questions.explanation: Excess nitrogen and phosphorus (from fertiliser runoff, sewage) fuel algal blooms; decomposing algae deplete dissolved oxygen → fish kills and dead zones. Remedy: reduce nutrient runoff, aerate water, biomanipulation.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The 'London-type smog' that caused the Great Smog of 1952 — a reducing smog formed under cool, damp conditions — is associated primarily with combustion of which fossil fuel?
questions.explanation: London-type smog is a sulphurous, reducing smog produced when coal is burned under cool, foggy conditions — high SO₂ converts in droplets to sulphuric acid. The Great Smog of December 1952 killed an estimated 4,000+ people and led to the UK's Clean Air Act 1956. The Los Angeles-type smog, by contrast, is an oxidising photochemical smog from vehicle emissions and sunlight.

questions.stem: Bharat Stage VI (BS-VI) emission norms — modelled on Euro 6 standards — became mandatory nationwide for all new vehicles sold in India from:
questions.explanation: India leapfrogged directly from BS-IV to BS-VI on 1 April 2020, skipping the intermediate BS-V stage. BS-VI cuts PM emissions from diesel engines by ~80% versus BS-IV and tightens NOx limits significantly. The move was driven by Delhi-NCR air-quality concerns and Supreme Court pressure.

questions.stem: The National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS), notified by the Central Pollution Control Board under the Air Act 1981, currently prescribe limits for how many distinct pollutants?
questions.explanation: The 2009 revision of NAAQS specifies standards for 12 pollutants: SO₂, NO₂, PM10, PM2.5, ozone (O₃), lead, carbon monoxide, ammonia, arsenic, nickel, benzene and benzo(a)pyrene. The previous (1994) version covered only 7. Uniform standards apply across industrial, residential and ecologically sensitive areas.

questions.stem: Crop-residue burning, the main contributor to Delhi-NCR's autumn smog episodes, is most intense in October-November in which adjoining pair of states?
questions.explanation: Stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana follows the kharif paddy harvest in late October-early November. The 15-20 day gap before rabi wheat sowing leaves farmers with massive paddy straw to clear; burning is cheapest. North-westerly winds carry the resulting smoke into Delhi-NCR, spiking PM2.5 levels.

questions.stem: If PM2.5 denotes particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter less than 2.5 micrometres, the term 'PM10' refers to particles less than:
questions.explanation: PM10 = particulate matter ≤ 10 µm aerodynamic diameter (coarse fraction, includes road dust, pollen). PM2.5 = particles ≤ 2.5 µm (fine fraction — penetrates alveoli, more damaging to health). NAAQS limit: PM10 60 µg/m³ annual, PM2.5 40 µg/m³ annual (Indian residential standard).

questions.stem: Minamata disease, a severe neurological syndrome caused by methylmercury bio-accumulating in fish after industrial discharge, first emerged in the 1950s in which country?
questions.explanation: Discovered in 1956 at Minamata Bay in Kumamoto Prefecture, Japan, the disease was caused by the Chisso Corporation's release of methylmercury-laden effluent into the bay; mercury concentrated in fish and shellfish eaten by locals. The 2013 Minamata Convention on Mercury — signed by India in 2014 and ratified in 2018 — is named after this incident.

questions.stem: The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), the apex statutory authority for pollution control in India, was originally constituted in 1974 under which Act of Parliament?
questions.explanation: The CPCB was established on 22 September 1974 under section 3 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. The same Board was later entrusted with air-pollution powers when the Air Act, 1981 was enacted, and with broader environmental functions under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The Wild Life Act 1972 set up an entirely separate institutional structure.
